Article.ArticleTitle: Cross-omics mapping of the human HIV restrictome across clinical states, immune-cell compartments, and protein responses.

Abstract.AbstractText: Host restriction factors can block HIV at multiple stages, but they are often studied as individual genes or within a single molecular layer. I performed an evidence-structured computational reanalysis of three independent public datasets to determine how the human HIV restrictome varies across clinical states, immune-cell compartments, and protein responses. The analysis used bulk monocyte RNA sequencing (GSE157198), PBMC single-cell/CITE-seq data (GSE256089), and primary CD4 T-cell proteomics (PXD012263) within a prespecified restrictome-immunometabolism framework. In GSE157198, ART-naive monocytes had higher core-restrictome activity than healthy controls (difference = 1.154, p = 0.000746), and core scores were strongly correlated with interferon/innate-sensing scores (Spearman r = 0.800, p = 7.47 × 10^-11). Core-lipid/cholesterol correlation was weaker and was not independent of interferon after conditional analysis. In GSE256089, participant-paired core-restrictome scores were enriched in NK cells relative to B cells, monocytes, and T cells, and matched random-gene-set analyses supported enrichment beyond background expression structure. FCGR3A monocytes also had higher participant-paired core scores than CD14 monocytes. Exploratory sensing/death-gene analysis identified cell-type-specific expression patterns but did not establish pathway activation, pyroptosis, or apoptosis. In PXD012263, the historical q < 0.05 proteomic selection contained 19 curated genes and retained mixed response polarity; sensitivity thresholds q < 0.01 and q < 0.10 selected 10 and 25 genes, respectively. Together, the results show that HIV restrictome activity varies across clinical and immune-cell contexts and is embedded within broader interferon-linked and immunometabolic states. Because the datasets are independent and not subject matched, the findings are observational and hypothesis-generating rather than causal.

Article.ArticleTitle: Fail-Closed Validation of Lineage-Associated Transcript-Count Diversity After IFN-β Stimulation in a Public Human PBMC Dataset.

Abstract.AbstractText: Shannon entropy of single-cell transcript counts reflects composition and sampling. We tested whether interferon-beta (IFN-β) stimulation was associated with donor-consistent diversity changes after employing technical controls. We reanalyzed GSE96583 peripheral blood mononuclear cells from eight donors with lupus, treating donors-not the 8949 target cells obtained from them-as inferential units. Analyses included sampling without replacement at 562 unique molecular identifiers, a 750-molecule sensitivity analysis, Miller-Madow correction, IFN-gene removal, and exact compositional decomposition. Mean paired-donor raw-count plug-in entropy increased by 0.138 bits in CD14+ monocytes and 0.329 bits in FCGR3A+ monocytes and decreased by 0.080 bits in natural killer cells. Directions persisted across prespecified robustness variants. Monocyte increases accompanied higher evenness and lower transcript dominance; natural killer cells showed the opposite pattern, without consistent richness changes. Adding IFN activity to donor-, condition-, and technical-covariate-adjusted models increased R2 by at most 0.0108. Entropy contributions strongly overlapped pseudobulk expression changes. In GSE194122, the implemented binary chromatin-accessibility entropy was determined by open-peak count, precluding biological cross-modality coupling claims. These findings support a lineage-divergent association within this single lupus cohort; independent replication is required before broader biological or diagnostic interpretation.
